analysis.one_liner: Requires pipeline operators to inspect lines near homes and sensitive areas, install safety valves, and certify operators.
analysis.headline: The House passed the Pipeline Safety Act of 1992 by voice vote on September 15, 1992, then set its own bill aside in favor of the Senate's companion bill, S. 1583.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill strengthens federal safety laws for natural gas and hazardous liquid pipelines. It requires operators to identify pipelines running through crowded neighborhoods and environmentally sensitive areas and inspect them regularly, including with internal inspection devices ('smart pigs'). It requires excess flow valves in new gas systems, certification of pipeline operators, periodic inspection of offshore and water-crossing pipelines, regulation of gathering lines, higher civil penalties, and criminal penalties for excavators who damage pipelines without following damage-prevention rules.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near pipelines in densely populated areas, communities near rivers and environmentally sensitive land, users of natural gas service, and coastal and waterfront residents exposed to offshore pipeline hazards. The environment benefits from mandatory corrective action when a pipeline endangers it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near pipelines and gas customers

how_it_helps.text: Makes federal pipeline safety standards mandatory for pipeline design, installation, inspection, testing, maintenance, and construction, where applying them was previously discretionary, and adds protection of the environment as an explicit goal of those standards.

Requires the Secretary of Transportation to issue rules identifying pipelines in high-density population areas and environmentally sensitive areas, and requiring periodic inspection of those lines, including with instrumented internal inspection devices.
Requires regulations prescribing when natural gas distribution systems must install excess flow valves, which limit gas release when a line is damaged.
Requires testing and certification of people who operate and maintain pipelines, specifically their ability to recognize abnormal operating conditions that may signal danger.
Extends periodic inspection to all offshore pipelines and other lines crossing navigable waters, and bars exempting offshore transfer pipelines from regulation.

Raises the maximum civil penalty from $10,000 to $25,000 and creates criminal penalties for excavators who damage pipelines after failing to use the one-call location system or ignoring pipeline markings.
Brings regulated gathering lines under federal oversight and adds environmental and independent public members to the technical safety standards committees.

analysis.who_pays: Pipeline operators — natural gas and hazardous liquid companies — bear the cost of inspections, smart pig equipment, valves, operator certification, and compliance monitoring, and they may pass some of these costs to customers through rates. Excavators and construction firms face new penalties for damaging pipelines. The bill also authorizes federal appropriations and small user fees capped at $500,000 a year.

drawbacks.text: The compliance costs fall on pipeline operators, who would be expected to pass much of the burden to customers through higher gas and fuel rates, and the bill's user-fee authority is capped at $500,000 a year, limiting industry cost-sharing for federal oversight.

The version passed by the House was softer than the bill originally introduced: it let the Secretary decide when smart-pig inspection is required instead of mandating instrumented inspection, and it directed only a survey of emergency flow restricting devices before any regulation requiring them.
Excess flow valve rules apply only to new systems or systems already being repaired, not retroactively to existing ones, so many older service lines stay unprotected.

An unrelated rider in the version that passed exempts certain rail-motor carrier mergers between November 1987 and May 1992 from the requirement that federal approval serve the public interest and not restrain competition.
Only state agencies with current federal certifications may adopt stricter intrastate pipeline safety standards than the federal program, which limits states that want to go further.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety benefits are targeted at the highest-risk pipelines — those near dense populations, rivers, and sensitive environments — and include flexibility (waivers, cost-based exceptions) that moderates the burden on operators. The main cost is compliance spending that customers will partly absorb through rates; the unrelated rail-merger rider and the softened inspection mandates are the clearest concessions to industry in an otherwise public-safety bill.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill by voice vote, then immediately laid it on the table in favor of the Senate's companion bill, S. 1583, which the record points to for final action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 19, 1991 by Rep. Philip Sharp with bipartisan cosponsors and referred jointly to the Energy and Commerce and Public Works and Transportation committees.

It took more than a year and two committee reports: Energy and Commerce reported it amended in October 1991 (Part I) and Public Works and Transportation reported it again in July 1992 (Part II), with the bill's name updated to the Pipeline Safety Act of 1992.
On September 15, 1992, Rep. Sharp moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill, a fast-track procedure requiring no recorded vote, and the House agreed by voice vote.
The House then laid the bill on the table, pointing further action to the Senate companion, S. 1583; the Senate never acted on H.R. 1489 itself.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one defeated the safety rules: the House cleared them without recorded opposition and steered final action to the Senate companion bill, so communities near pipelines kept the prospect of stronger rules rather than seeing the bill buried.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities near pipelines; the Senate companion carried on

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, saw it through two committee markups, and moved to suspend the rules and pass it on the House floor.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings and markups and reported the bill amended, H. Rept. 102-247 Part I.

for.name: House Public Works and Transportation Committee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings and markups and reported the bill amended, H. Rept. 102-247 Part II, and placed it on the Union Calendar.

against.name: United States Senate (102nd Congress)
against.role: Chamber that never took up the House bill
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on H.R. 1489; the House laid its bill on the table pointing further action to the Senate companion, S. 1583.

sides.party_line_note: No recorded opposition appears anywhere in the action history: the bill passed the House by voice vote, and its six cosponsors split 5 Democrats and 1 Republican.

industries.industry: Natural gas and hazardous liquid pipeline operators
industries.note: The bill imposes mandatory inspections, smart-pig use in populated and sensitive areas, excess flow valves, operator certification, and higher penalties, with compliance costs operators would partly pass to customers. Their interest in avoiding those costs ran directly against the safety and environmental protections the public gains.

They must install excess flow valves in new or repaired systems and notify customers, but the passed version dropped a provision that would have required them to maintain customer-owned service lines up to the building wall, requiring only that they advise customers instead.

industries.industry: Railroads and motor carriers involved in 1987–1992 mergers
industries.note: A rider in the passed version retroactively exempts certain rail-motor carrier mergers from the Interstate Commerce Commission's public-interest and competition review — a benefit unrelated to pipeline safety.
Mandatory periodic internal inspection of high-risk pipelines creates demand for inspection devices, and the bill funds development of a device that can detect seam failures.

They face civil and criminal penalties for damaging pipelines without using the one-call system, but they also benefit from required operator marking of pipeline locations, which prevents costly and dangerous strikes.
